name: Nominalisation in formal writing
subtitle: In formal writing, verbs and adjectives often become nouns: decide → decision, available → availability. A noun phrase such as a sharp rise in prices says what a whole clause says, but more briefly. Spoken English keeps the verbs.
source: icanspeak Spanish original English text (grammar-c1 run, 2026-10-29)

concept.exampleHtml: Prices rose sharply, so many families cut their spending. · The sharp rise in prices led many families to cut their spending.

qa.html: Many nouns are made with a suffix: -ion (decide → decision, reduce → reduction), -ment (develop → development), -ure (fail → failure), -al (arrive → arrival, refuse → refusal), -ance / -ence (perform → performance). Some verbs do not change: increase → an increase, cut → a cut. A few change completely: grow → growth, choose → choice. Adjectives often take -ity or -ness: available → availability, safe → safety.

A noun brings a preposition with it. The preposition depends on the noun: a rise in prices, a decision to close, a demand for housing, an investigation into the fire, the cause of the delay. The thing that changes or is affected comes after of or in: Prices rose. → the rise in prices. Experts examined the data. → the examination of the data (by experts).

Nominalisation often needs a verb that fits the noun: make a decision, reach an agreement, carry out an investigation, give an explanation. Or you use There has been: Prices have risen sharply. → There has been a sharp rise in prices. The adverb becomes an adjective: react quickly → a quick reaction.

The noun style is short and serious, but it can be heavy. Too many nouns in a row (the implementation of the evaluation of the reduction of costs) are hard to read. Turn one noun back into a verb: They evaluated how the costs were reduced. Use nouns in reports, news and academic writing. Use verbs in speech, emails and simple explanations.

Typical mistakes: ✗ the decide of the board → ✓ the decision of the board (use the noun form) · ✗ an increase of prices → ✓ an increase in prices (in for what changes; of for the amount: an increase of 5 per cent) · ✗ a demand of housing → ✓ a demand for housing (learn the noun with its preposition)

concept.noteHtml: Which style when? Formal writing (reports, news, academic texts) likes nouns. Speech prefers verbs: We decided to close it sounds natural, The decision to close it was taken sounds like a report. The noun style also hides who did something, like the passive (see the passive). To build the nouns, see noun suffixes. Fixed pairs like make a decision are in verb + noun collocations. For of or 's see 's or of. For the prepositions that often start such phrases (due to, despite) see formal prepositions.

Example
rows: The availability of rooms is limited.
Her ability to learn fast impressed us.
The safety of the bridge is a concern.
The strength of the economy surprised experts.
The efficiency of the system has improved.

tables.caption: Verbal style and noun style
head: Verbal style (speech)
Noun style (formal writing)
rows: There has been a sharp rise in prices.
They decided to close the plant.
The decision to close the plant was criticised.
The committee examined the data carefully.
The committee carried out a careful examination of the data.
The firm introduced the scheme, and costs fell.
The introduction of the scheme led to a fall in costs.

boxes.badge: Verbs that go with the noun
items: make a decision, reach an agreement
There has been a sharp rise in …

listen.text: There has been a sharp rise in the price of fuel.
listen.note: Noun style: a sharp rise in = the price of fuel has risen sharply.

listen.text: The decision to close the plant was criticised.
listen.note: decision to + verb. The verbal style is They decided to close the plant.

listen.text: The company's failure to respond caused a delay.
listen.note: failure to + verb: the company did not respond.

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose what you hear. You can listen twice.

items.text: There has been a sharp rise in unemployment.
The decision to close the library surprised everyone.
choices: The decision to close the library
The discussion to close the library
The division to close the library

items.text: Her failure to reply caused a delay.
The reduction in costs was welcome.
The availability of rooms is limited.
An investigation into the accident is under way.

rounds.label: 1 · verb → noun phrase
rounds.instruction: You hear a short sentence with a verb. Say it in the noun style: There was / has been + adjective + noun + in.

example.answer: There has been a rise in unemployment.

items.answer: There has been a sharp rise in prices.
There was a quick fall in sales.
There was a slight increase in traffic.
There was strong growth in demand.
There was slow growth in the population.
There was a sudden fall in prices.

rounds.label: 2 · verb + noun → one verb
rounds.instruction: You hear a formal phrase with a verb and a noun. Say it again with one plain verb.

items.prompt: She made an attempt to climb.
